newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto dismissal upheld, Pakistan polls go ahead.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto dismissal upheld, Pakistan polls go ahead.

text.p: Pakistan's Supreme Court upheld the dismissal of prime minister Benazir Bhutto on Wednesday, clearing the way for elections that pollsters say she will lose.

"There is enough material to establish corruption, nepotism and misrule," Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah said at the end of a hearing which began on January 13 into Bhutto's appeal against her dismissal by President Farooq Leghari.
"We uphold the order," he said of Leghari's November 5 dismissal of Bhutto on a range of charges. She denies them all.

The verdict means national and provincial assembly elections will go ahead on Monday as scheduled, with Bhutto's arch-foe, former prime minister Nawaz Sharif of the Pakistan Moslem League (PML), a clear front-runner.
The latest opinion poll, by Gallup Pakistan and published in The News English-language daily, said 40 percent of its 2,000 respondents across the country planned to vote for the PML.
It said just 20 percent planned to vote for Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) now, although it expected that figure to rise five to 10 points by election day.
Bhutto shrugged off the Supreme Court ruling.
"This is nothing unexpected. I knew they were going to give a decision against us," she told a news conference at her home in the southern city of Karachi during a break from election campaigning.
"Every time the Bhutto family goes to the court, the decision is different. Every time the decision for the Bhuttos is unfavourable," she said.

The PML was happy. "The PML feels that with this Supreme Court verdict, all the confusion that was sought to be created in the present political situation will now be clear and elections can be held on schedule," a party spokesman said.
Witnesses said police clashed with Bhutto supporters outside the court in Islamabad soon after the verdict was announced.
They said police baton-charged stone-throwing demonstrators who were chanting pro-Bhutto slogans and the violence fizzled out. There was no immediate word on injuries or arrests.
The Supreme Court's keenly-awaited judgement, by a 6-1 majority of the seven-judge bench, was applauded by businessmen and the markets.

The caretaker government installed by Leghari complained it had inherited an economy in severe crisis from the Bhutto administration, saying Pakistan had lost credibility with international lenders and investors.
"The judgement is good for the country and the economy," said Maqbool Sadiq, chairman of the Karachi Cotton Association.
"The judgement should now remove uncertainty and the nation should work to strengthen the economy," said Younas Khan, country chief of Deutsche Bank.

The stock market index in Karachi, Pakistan's commercial capital, rose 11.11 points, or 0.74 percent, on Wednesday and traders said speculators had moved it on hopes of the verdict going against Bhutto.
Brokers said prices surged in after-hours trading following the Supreme Court ruling.
They said prices were likely to go on rising on Thursday and some predicted that the Karachi 100-share index could rise another 70 points.
